```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(mediaplanr)
```

An agentic media planner is a language model that edits a media plan: it
reads the plan, proposes changes, has them scored, checks them, and hands
them to a person to approve. `mediaplanr` is the part of that system that
holds the plan and decides what is allowed. This vignette runs the loop once,
on the agency plan from `vignette("getting_started")`, with real calls.

Three owners, one job each:

| | Owns | In this loop |
|---|---|---|
| `mediaplanr` | plan state, legal actions, constraints, checks, history | describe, validate, derive, check, record |
| `mrmopt` | scoring and optimization | score |
| the app | the agent loop and the human approval gate | propose, approve |

The loop:

```
describe  ->  propose ops  ->  validate & derive  ->  score  ->  check
          ->  record why   ->  a person approves
```

## The plan, and what the agent is told

The approved plan, the response models fitted to it, and the rules it lives
under:

```{r}
ext <- function(file) system.file("extdata", file, package = "mediaplanr")

plan <- media_plan_from_df(
  read.csv(ext("agency_plan.csv")),
  grain       = c("channel", "partner", "campaign", "tactic"),
  time        = "month",
  name        = "National digital, Q4 2026 - Q1 2027",
  nickname    = "Rev 1",
  spend_basis = "media_net",
  status      = "approved",
  approved_on = "2026-09-15"
)
models <- read.csv(ext("agency_models.csv"))
rules  <- plan_constraints(read.csv(ext("agency_constraints.csv")),
                           name = "Agency guardrails")
```

### What the plan looks like

The agent does not read 54 rows -- or 50,000. It reads `describe_plan()`: a
summary capped at `top_n` values per list, so it is the same size however big
the plan is, and every number in it reconciles to the plan's rows.

```{r}
description <- describe_plan(plan, top_n = 3, models = models,
                             constraints = rules, reference = plan)
nchar(jsonlite::toJSON(description, auto_unbox = TRUE))
```

The sections that matter most before an edit: what cannot move, which rules
are tight, and what the models cannot score.

```{r}
jsonlite::toJSON(description[c("commitments", "constraints", "models")],
                 auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
```

`headroom` is the spend an edit could take out at all. The upfront's
`fixed_total` is `binding`: it holds with no slack, so nothing may move it.

### What the agent may send

The agent edits only through operations, and `plan_ops_schema()` is the
contract: a JSON Schema for the list of ops, narrowed to this plan. Given as
the type of a tool's argument, it stops a malformed op before it reaches R.
A `target` may name only the plan's columns and values:

```{r}
schema <- plan_ops_schema(plan)
transfer <- Filter(function(op) op$title == "transfer", schema$items$oneOf)[[1]]
unlist(transfer$properties$to$properties$partner$anyOf[[1]]$enum)
```

## The agent proposes

Asked to lift prospecting reach in Q1 without touching commitments, the
agent replies with two transfers, as JSON:

```{r}
reply <- r"([
  {"transfer": 30000,
   "from": {"channel": "Streaming"},
   "to":   {"partner": "DSP A", "tactic": "Prospecting"},
   "during": {"from": "2027-01-01", "to": "2027-03-31"}},
  {"transfer": 20000,
   "from": {"partner": "DSP B"},
   "to":   {"partner": "Video A", "tactic": "Prospecting"},
   "during": {"from": "2027-01-01", "to": "2027-03-31"}}
])"
ops <- jsonlite::fromJSON(reply, simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

(`simplifyVector = FALSE` matters: simplifying would turn the list of ops
into a data frame, which `build_scenario()` reads as an allocation.)

### Validate and derive

`build_scenario()` checks every op and derives a new scenario. The approved
plan is never touched. This proposal is refused:

```{r, error = TRUE}
build_scenario(plan, edits = ops, name = "Q1 prospecting push")
```

DSP B has a floor of 15,000 a month; in Q1 it can give 17,500, not 20,000.
The refusal is specific enough to act on, and that is the point: the agent
did not have to be told about the floor. It is a fact in the plan, and every
edit respects it. The agent asks for what can be given, and records why:

```{r}
ops[[2]]$transfer <- 15000

proposal <- build_scenario(
  plan,
  edits     = ops,
  name      = "National digital, Q4 2026 - Q1 2027",
  nickname  = "Q1 prospecting push",
  objective = "More prospecting reach in Q1",
  rationale = list(author = "agent",
                   goal = "lift Q1 prospecting reach without touching commitments",
                   constraints_id = rules@id)
)
```

The 30,000 out of Streaming came from Stream B alone: Stream A's upfront is
committed, so the transfer routed around it.

## Score

Scoring is `mrmopt`'s job. `mediaplanr` hands it the spend each response
model scores, period by period -- with unmodeled spend kept, so nothing is
silently left out of the total:

```{r, warning = FALSE}
weekly <- spend_by_model(proposal, models, basis = "week")
head(weekly, 3)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# `fits`: models from mrmopt::fit_response(), named by model_id
scored <- split(weekly, weekly$model_id)
kpi <- vapply(names(scored), function(id) {
  f <- mrmopt::mrm_response_function(fits[[id]])
  sum(f(scored[[id]]$planned_spend))
}, numeric(1))
```

## Check

The proposal respected every row's bounds -- it could not have been built
otherwise. The group rules are checked against the approved plan:

```{r}
check_constraints(proposal, rules, reference = plan)[
  , c("type", "target", "actual", "slack", "ok")]
```

Every rule holds. The signed budget is another matter: moving money between
channels moves it between their Q1 envelopes too.

```{r}
q1_budget <- data.frame(
  channel = c("Streaming", "Programmatic", "Online Video"),
  from = "2027-01-01", to = "2027-03-31",
  amount = c(250000, 212500, 87750)
)
check_budget(proposal, q1_budget)
```

Both checks warn rather than refuse. They are for the person who approves the
plan: the agent's proposal is legal, and these say what signing it would
mean.

## Record and hand over

The proposal goes to review with what scoring returned (illustrative figures
here) added to its rationale. The package never computes a forecast; it
keeps the one it was given.

```{r}
proposal <- revise(
  proposal,
  status    = "to review",
  rationale = c(proposal@rationale,
                list(forecast = list(conversions = 18450, roas = 2.4)))
)

set <- add_scenario(scenario_set(plan), proposal)
edit_log(set)[, c("scenario", "author", "op", "target", "to", "amount", "window")]
compare_scenarios(set, against = "current_approved")[
  , c("scenario", "total_planned_spend", "spend_vs_current_approved")]
```

`edit_log()` is exactly what was applied: the scenario was derived by
replaying that record, so it cannot have drifted from it. Approval is the
person's: `revise(status = "approved", approved_on = )`, after which
`current_approved()` names the new plan and the next loop starts from it.

## What the agent may and may not do

**May:** read the plan through `describe_plan()`; propose any operation in
`plan_ops_schema()`; derive as many scenarios as it likes -- each is a new
object, and the plan it came from is never changed; check its own proposals
with `check_constraints()` and `check_budget()`.

**May not:**

- **Move money that cannot move.** Spend bounds are in the plan, and every
  edit respects them: an edit across a group routes around a bound, and one
  that names a row's value outright is refused at it.
- **Change a commitment quietly.** Bounds change only through the `rebound`
  op, which shows in `edit_log()` like any other edit.
- **Send something malformed or vague.** A typo in a target is an error
  naming the alternatives, never a silent no-op; ops are checked whether they
  came from JSON, a constructor or by hand.
- **Approve its own work.** The package records approval; the app decides
  who may give it.

## Why commitments live in the plan

An agent could be told about the upfront commitment in its prompt. Prompts
are read, mostly, and followed, usually. A commitment stored as `min_spend`
and `max_spend` on the plan's rows is not read by anyone: every edit path --
an agent's op, a planner's allocation, an optimizer's output -- passes
through the same check, so the commitment holds whoever is editing and
however carefully they were told. The rules about groups of rows are the
same idea one level up: written once in a `PlanConstraints`, checked the same
way by the agent and, next, by the optimizer.
